newsitem.title: INDIA: India oil payments crunch bites,eyes on government.
newsitem.headline: India oil payments crunch bites,eyes on government.

text.p: A payments crunch in the Indian oil industry has led to arguments over which companies are best positioned to borrow cash to keep crude supplies coming, oil industry officials said on Thursday.
The row boils down to whether the government will act decisively to repay state-owned oil companies money owed for supporting subsidised petroleum prices.
The ruling United Front coalition is meeting for the third time on Sunday in a bid to find an answer.
"The critical point is the meeting of the steering committee on June 15. We are hoping for some way in which we get our money back quickly," a spokesman for state-owned Indian Oil Corp said.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Finance Minister P.Chidambaram have pressed for price increases, while left parties in the coalition want alternatives to be considered. A decision has been deferred several times already.
"We're hoping something comes out of this meeting. We can't be endlessly in this situation," another Indian refiner said.

The companies at the end of March were owed 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) from the oil pool account deficit, which represents money owed by the government to companies for selling below market prices.

The oil subsidy bill in fiscal 1997/98 totalled around 180 billion rupees -- which includes the cost of both products sold below market prices plus a cross-subsidisation element under which some products, like gasoline, are priced above market prices.
Subsidies, which have strong political protection, will be around for some time despite long term plans to align domestic prices with international levels.
But oil companies are asking why they should continue to carry the burden.
"If subsidies have to be given then it should come from the government budget, as food subsidies do. Why whould the subsidy fall on product prices?" one oil company source commented.

IOC, which is the sole importer of crude into India and is owed around 100 billion rupees ($2.79 billion) by the government, has asked the Petroleum Ministry to put pressure on refiners to repay oustanding bills for feedstock supplied to them.
"We have only requested the Petroleum Ministry to tell them to make payments before we take any other action," the IOC official said.
IOC, which imported 30 million tonnes of crude in 1996/97 and has a refining capacity of 24.6 million, says it has not yet exhausted its $3.5 billion external commercial borrowing limit.
But the money will run out if action is not taken to whittle down the oil pool deficit. And a debt/equity ratio of two to one will limit IOC's ability to go to the market.
Cochin Refinery Ltd is planning to pay IOC soon.
"Now for paying IOC we are planning to borrow for six months," a senior Cochin Refinery official told Reuters. He said the company will seek between 500 and 600 million rupees.
Some refiners say they cannot pay until the OCC pays them.
Mangalore Refineries and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL) owes IOC between four to five billion rupees ($114-140), officials said.
MRPL has a debt/equity ratio of four to one, and has already borrowed 10 billion rupees ($279 million) to cover operational spending -- notably feedstock purchases.
"We don't have many other avenues to raise loans," a senior MRPL official said. ($1.00=35.8)
